newsitem.title: USA: Reno apologizes to cleared Olympic bombing suspect.
newsitem.headline: Reno apologizes to cleared Olympic bombing suspect.

text.p: U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno apologised on Thursday to former Olympic bombing suspect Richard Jewell for news leaks that put him in the public spotlight.

"I think we owe him an apology," Reno said at her weekly Justice Department news conference. "We should insure that there be no leaks. And I regret very much the leak that made him an object of so much public attention."

Jewell, who was working as a security guard, discovered a backpack containing the pipe bomb that exploded during the Atlanta Olympic Games, killing one person and injuring more than 100. A cameraman also died of a heart attack at the scene.
He initially was hailed as a hero. But after news leaks to the media, he then became the only named suspect in the investigation, although he never was charged with any crime.
After being hounded by the FBI and the news media for 88 days, Jewell in October finally was cleared by the Justice Department of any suspicion in the bombing.

"I don't think any apology is sufficient when somebody has gone through ... what Mr. Jewell has gone through. And what I need to do is to make sure that we take steps to try to avoid something like that in the future," Reno said.
Reno said she would be happy to talk to Jewell, but had yet to send him a formal written apology.
She made clear she was apologising only for the news leak, not the way FBI agents questioned Jewell after the bombing.

A Justice Department report released on Monday found that FBI agents in Atlanta made a major error when they questioned Jewell, who did not know he was a suspect, under the guise that they were making a training video.
The ploy could have violated Jewell's constitutional rights and could have invalidated any information provided during the questioning, the report concluded.
"What I'm concerned about is that he was the subject of such public attention. I don't think that's right. With respect to the other issues, the ... report should speak for itself," Reno said.
Jewell told a congressional committee on Wednesday that FBI agents tried to publicly humilate him when he was a suspect.

"Not only did the FBI accuse the wrong man, its agents in Atlanta and its officials in Washington actively participated in publicly humiliating me and privately violating my constitutional rights," he said.
Jewell said the FBI knew within a few days after his name was leaked to the media that it "had a public relations disaster on its hands," and that it had the wrong suspect.

A number of Republican and Democratic members of Congress have been increasingly critical at hearings this week over the way the FBI and the Justice Department -- agencies which Reno is responsible for -- have handled the case.
The Justice Department and the FBI also have conducted an investigation to try to determine the source of the leak, but have been unsuccessful.
Jewell on Thursday sued a New York radio station, charging that one of its talk show hosts libelled him.
Jewell alleged that the host, who went by the single name of Lionel, broadcast a series of false and defamatory statements in the days following the bombing.
A spokeswoman for ABC said the company had no comment.
According to the lawsuit, Lionel said in a broadcast on July 31, 1996: "He did it... He probably did it."
